scoreNote: Between Adequate and Strong (4.5): grants that breadth genuinely educates while showing it is one route among several rather than the best; clear and well organized, though it treads familiar ground.

sentences.text: Everyone agrees we want students to become truly educated, but how best to get there is far from settled.
The statement offers one confident answer: that requiring university students to take courses outside their major is the best way to ensure a true education.
Breadth of study genuinely helps make a person educated, but the statement overstates its case, because requiring outside courses is one valuable means among several, not the single best way.
It is true that studying beyond one's major contributes a great deal to becoming truly educated.

A person who knows only one field sees the world through a single lens, while one exposed to several can connect ideas, weigh different ways of thinking, and avoid the narrowness of pure specialization.
An engineer who has studied some history and ethics, or a poet who understands a little science, brings a fuller mind to whatever they do.
Real problems cross the boundaries between subjects, so a broadly educated person is better equipped for the mixed questions of life and work.
So the statement is right that breadth matters, and required outside courses are a sensible way to encourage it.
A mind confined to one subject is only half furnished.

sections.role: Body — But it is not the best way

sentences.text: However, to call required outside courses the best way to ensure a true education claims far too much.
Being truly educated is not the same as having sampled many subjects; it involves judgment, depth, and the ability to think, which a scattering of outside courses does not guarantee.
A student could take a dozen unrelated classes and remain shallow in all of them, mistaking exposure for understanding.
Other paths may matter more: mastering a single field deeply teaches rigor and how knowledge is built, and learning to think critically can be done within one subject or across many.
Some of the most truly educated people the world has known were deep specialists, not dabblers in everything.
Breadth is one route to a real education, but to crown it the best ignores the equal claims of depth and good teaching.

sections.role: Body — True education has many sources

sentences.text: Moreover, what truly educates a person is rarely a single requirement but a combination of forces.
Inspiring teachers, the habit of questioning, deep engagement with at least one subject, and breadth across several all contribute, and no one of them is sufficient alone.
A required survey course taken without interest may leave a student no more educated than before, while a single great mentor can transform one entirely.
To single out one method as the best misunderstands how complex and personal a real education is.
There is no one road to an educated mind, only many that must be travelled together.
In conclusion, requiring courses outside the major helps make students educated but is not the single best way to ensure it.

Breadth is valuable, yet depth, good teaching, and the habit of critical thought matter at least as much, so a true education comes from their combination rather than from any one requirement crowned above the rest.
Require breadth by all means, but do not mistake one good ingredient for the whole recipe of an educated mind.
